analytic.title: Fitting Schedulability Analysis Theory into Model-Driven Engineering

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The theory behind state-of-the-art schedulability analysis has reached such a level of sophistication that its complete mastering by the average industrial practitioner is practically infeasible. The centrality of automation promoted by model-driven engineering may facilitate the uptake of the front-end of the analysis theory by the industrial world. In this paper we qualitatively evaluate how current approaches to model-based schedulability analysis may employ and feed state-of-the-art analysis equations; we then illustrate a new strategy which, by way of model transformation, warrants a high degree of confidence in and permits an iterative refinement of the input to sophisticated analysis equations. We contend that model-driven engineering is well suited for fitting the most advanced analysis theories and to chart the course for future improvements in the area of model-based schedulability analysis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Model-driven engineering (MDE, [21]) has recently emerged as a major research area in software engineering. MDE wants to move the hub of the development process from the source code toward a more abstract level of specification languages, agnostic on implementation details and more easily amenable to the evaluation of system properties: in other words, to model. A model encompasses the system and software architecture, the relevant action semantics and the deployment information. The implementation, possibly along with validation and analysis, of a model is obtained through a chain of model transformations that take the model to increasingly lower-abstraction representation: a typical example of a model transformation is automated code generation, which perfectly mirrors the compilation process typical of source-centered development.

Whilst the model-driven approach and technology have earned some success in enterprise computing [8], they have yet to gain acceptance in the real-time domain, albeit their fitness for purpose has already been argued for [10]. In this paper we look at whether and how conveniently schedulability analysis can marry with the model-driven development of real-time systems. The present time is favorable for such an evaluation for several reasons: first, the industrial community is steadily moving toward MDE: important projects and collaborative initiatives (for example TOP-CASED 1 , Papyrus2 , and ASSERT 3 ) ostensibly confirm this trend; secondly, the theory of schedulability analysis has advanced to such a level of sophistication that its full understanding by the average engineer and its manual application is simply untenable: the emphasis of MDE on automation is an excellent opportunity to break state-of-the-art analysis techniques to the industrial world; and, finally, technology presently exists that permit affordable development of tools to explore, exploit and evaluate model-driven approaches. In addition to scrutinizing current approaches to this problem, this paper discusses a new strategy to modelbased analysis which has proven able to produce a quantifiable improvement to real-life industrial processes in terms of automation, consistency and accuracy. We evaluate our proposed strategy against:

• The amount of information to be supplied by the user in order for model-based analysis to apply • Whether and how the detail of information demanded by schedulability analysis can be derived from the model without frustrating the MDE tension high levels of abstraction • What risks of coarse and thus inaccurate or pessimistic analysis may be incurred from adoption of the MDE paradigm and how they can be defeated.

div.head: Related work
div.p: Model-based schedulability analysis revolves around the concept of the Schedulability Analysis Model (SAM), a model that represents the system design in terms which can be directly related to the chosen theory of analysis and its equations; the modeling language should then be capable of expressing the SAM semantics directly. The SAM is then used to feed up the equations to determine the timing properties of the system. The modeling languages we review in this section have two characteristics of interest: they have been recently used in either production systems or in industrial research projects and have the critical mass to impact the development process of next-generation systems. For a modeling language to qualify for use in an MDE setting for real-time systems, we require that it must have been used for: system modeling; model-based analysis, and automated code generation. The modeling languages we consider are: UML2 and its profiles [14]; AADL [20]; and MARTE [14]; we also discuss our own effort, RCM, a modeling infrastructure developed at the University of Padua within the ASSERT project (see the Acknowledgments). This infrastructure includes a graphical modeling language and its editor, a model validator and a set of model transformations to feed model-based analysis and code generation, all integrated in a single Eclipse plug-in [6].
In the following, we shall use the RCM acronym extensively to denote our modeling infrastructure as a whole.

div.head: UML2 and SysML
div.p: UML2 is a multi-purpose modeling language developed within the OMG consortium. The initial focus of UML2 was to model the software architecture and its action semantics. The OMG has recently extended UML2 with SysML to encompass system modeling [14].

Most UML2 tools are implemented on the UML2 metamodel enacted by OMG, which fully and formally defines the language syntax and semantics. UML2 provides an extension mechanism in the form of profiles, which are defined in terms of stereotypes (via inheritance at metaclass level), tags and constraints. The latter are expressed in OCL [14], a formal textual language, which allows the portable specification of (meta)modeling constraints.

UML2 models are represented as XML files obeying to a schema which maps the OMG specification [14]. The core modeling technology permits to exploit all of the latest OMG-related technologies for modeling and model transformation, such as those developed within the Generative Modeling Framework on the Eclipse platform: those technologies are a de-facto standard for industrial and research projects in the model-driven arena.
The main drawbacks of UML2 and SysML when it comes to modeling and analyzing real-time systems are:

1. They do not recognize all elements of the SAM (process, shared resources, scheduling policy, etc.) as primitive entities of the metamodel 2. The consistency between multiple views of a given model (including the SAM) is left under the responsi-bility of the user, who may possibly resort to the specification of ad-hoc OCL constraints.

The lack of standard support to map the SAM semantics rooted in the theory of schedulability analysis forces the user to rely on local dialects to express the SAM required to feed their analysis equations: as a result, tools for model-based analysis cannot rely on a well-defined input format (endangering the integrity of the model syntax and semantics across implementations).

UML2 is widely used in mainstream software engineering, but the aforementioned drawbacks have prevented its use for more than architectural and functional modeling in the domain of interest. The final draft specification of SysML has been recently approved by OMG and it is already supported by several industrial and research tools.

div.head: AADL
div.p: AADL (Architecture Analysis and Design Language, [20]) is a system modeling language specifically tailored for real-time embedded systems. In contrast with UML2 which is graphical, AADL is based on textual specification: the core modeling technology of AADL uses parsers and compilers, much like normal programming languages. AADL focuses on the modeling and analysis of architecture and execution platforms by describing threads, processes, processors and their interactions. In terms of system modeling, the expressive power and semantics of AADL are comparable to those of SysML.

Unlike UML2, the AADL standard includes primitive entities to map SAM-related semantics (e.g.: processes, tasks, and shared resources); unfortunately, AADL does not define an extensible SAM framework. Moreover, AADL does not provide standard facilities to model the execution platform (run-time kernel and its metrics; for example the cost of accessing a shared resource under the immediate priority ceiling protocol). Dialects have been proposed to overcome this limit: for example Cheddar [22], which extends AADL with a property set (conceptually similar to a UML2 profile) specifying the syntax to describe a system for the purposes of schedulability analysis and simulation. No such dialect however is part of the standard; and since the language does not provide any way to formally express constraints (in the way of OCL), the semantics of any language extensions in that direction is only informal.
The main drawbacks of AADL for model-driven engineering of real-time systems are:

1. The definition of the run-time semantics of AADL entities is (perhaps intentionally) open to interpretation, which makes it difficult for the model to be a faithful representation of the run-time system. For example, the run-time semantics of component interaction through ports is defined in the optional Behavior Annex and only in part 2. The lack of attention for functional modeling: the recent addition of a behavioral annex in the form of a textual description of hierarchical state machines does not match the expressive power and availability of UML2

div.head: MARTE
div.p: MARTE [14] is a UML2 profile enacted by the OMG to cover the modeling of real-time systems. MARTE defines a general framework for schedulability analysis and a set of facilities to annotate models, which supersede the UML profile for Schedulability, Performance and Time [14].

Much like AADL, MARTE includes the primitive entities required to capture SAM-related semantics. Unlike the other modeling languages discussed in this paper, however, MARTE formally specifies the syntax and the semantics of those entities and does it within a standard framework. A further MARTE feature of interest is the support for modeling the execution platform (operating system, kernel, middleware, etc.) in terms of primitive language constructs: model transformation can thus use that information to turn platform-independent models (PIM) into platform-specific ones (PSM). The resulting PSM may thus contain all of the information needed to perform accurate, fine-grained schedulability analysis at model level.

Thanks to OCL, MARTE can be deployed on top of any UML2 implementation: the validation of UML2 models against MARTE constraints is identical to the validation performed under any other UML2 profile. In this respect, the only important limitation of MARTE in our view is the lack of consistency enforcement across multiple views of the system: the profile itself does in fact not guarantee that the model used for schedulability analysis be consistent with the model used for software modeling and code generation. This limit proceeds from the UML2 inheritance of MARTE. MARTE is currently implemented on top of only a few industrial and research UML2 tools, but the support for it is expected to grow fast.

div.head: RCM: seeking consistency and accuracy
div.p: From the discussion in section 2 we may argue that the combination of MARTE and SysML offers the best tradeoff in terms of expressive power, domain fitness, semantic consistency and industrial support. Yet, those two languages form a vast mass for industrial practitioners to master and command. Furthermore, they require the user to explicitly model the SAM and to manually guarantee the consistency of the latter with the design model as specified in terms of software entities, action specification and use relations. The absence of automated enforcement of consistency challenges the desire to exploit the theory of scheduling analysis by raising two key questions:

• Does the SAM correctly represent the user model in terms of software components, interactions and execution flows? • What confidence can be placed in the results of the analysis and what do they signify for the user model and for the system at run time respectively?
To address those concerns in the ASSERT project we developed RCM [3], a modeling language for high-integrity, distributed, real-time systems.

div.head: User modeling semantics
div.p: The modeling language at the core of RCM is UML2-like and covers: functional modeling by class diagrams and state machines augmented with an action language; system modeling through component diagrams; and system deployment by processor-level hardware modeling and the allocation of software entities to computational nodes.

RCM strictly separates sequential and concurrencyrelated modeling: views which serve for sequential modeling (class and state machine diagrams) are disallowed to use concurrency and time-related semantics. The latter elements of the specification are expressed declaratively, via a suite of stereotypes attached to components services, to require for example the use of a synchronization protocol to protect a shared resource against concurrent access or to cause a task release on invocation of a given interface. The reasons why we enforce such a strict separation of concerns are manifold. To begin with, in this way we allow the most appropriate verification tool to be selected and applied for each view of the model. We furthermore permit the reuse of functional specifications across distinct concurrent and distribution architectures (which would not be possible if the former included specific concurrency semantics) and, symmetrically, the reuse of the latter with alternate implementations of the functional specification.

The semantics of the RCM metamodel may be traced to a UML2 profile. We however opted for implementing our own metamodel, yet inspired on UML2: our approach follows the so-called heavy-weight metamodeling strategy [8], because we did not only extend the semantics of the core UML2 metamodel, but we also added new relations across metamodel entities. The heavy-weight strategy permits an easier development of model validators and model transformations because all of the information required by the relevant tools can be directly embedded in the model instead of being calculated or inferred at the time of validation and/or transformation. Unfortunately, metamodels designed with the heavy-weight approach cannot be implemented on top of existing UML2 tools: for this reason we had to develop our own graphical editor. We were careful however to ensure that our heavy-weight implementation strategy would not preclude future conversion of RCM to a full UML2/MARTE profile.

div.head: Computational model
div.p: In order for model-based analysis to be trustworthy, the SAM must prove to be a faithful representation of the system at run time as generated from the user model. Our computational model of choice is the Ravenscar Computational Model (RP in the following), which directly emanates in language-neutral terms from the Ada Ravenscar Profile [4].

There are at least three good reasons for adopt the RP as the abstraction of the run-time environment of a real-time system: (i) the RP guarantees that the timing behavior of the system is deterministic and amenable to static analysis; (ii) the RP has been proven to be expressive enough to model real-world applications in the domain of interest; and (iii) industrial-quality implementations exist for it, in particular as part of the Ada 2005 language and as a restriction of the Real-Time Specification for Java. An implementation of the RP (in the form of a compiler and run-time kernel) is expected to reject semantics that fail the Ravenscar restrictions and to ensure that programs at run time execute within the boundary concurrency behavior as analyzed.

In our proof-of-concept demonstrator we constrained the RCM metamodel semantics to support a single computational model. Our choice resembles that of the Esterel language (implemented in the SCADE toolset [7]) in the world of synchronous programming. By supporting and enforcing a single computational model, we obtain that:

1. The user can only use legal entities (which provably abide by the chosen computational model) to populate the model 2. There is a specific and strictly preserved semantic relation between every model entity and the source code generated from them (with code generation being no other than another form of rule-based model transformation governed)

3. The computational model that informs the model development is fully consistent with that which underpins the mathematical equations which are used to predict the schedulability behavior of the system.

In the RP, threaded objects (tasks) are restricted to have a single activation event, and cyclic or sporadic execution behavior. Tasks do not interact with one another directly, but their communications are mediated by protected objects. Protected objects are shared resources equipped with a synchronization protocol in the form of the priority ceiling protocol or equivalently the stack-based policy [1]. Those protocols guarantee mutual exclusion, bounded priority inversion and structural absence of deadlock.

Adopting the RP further permits to characterize with fine-grained accuracy the semantics and the timing overhead of the kernel mechanisms that govern or influence the scheduling of tasks in the system [25] and also to allow the implementation of run-time kernels to incur a small footprint in size and an equally small overhead in time.

div.head: Software architecture
div.p: The architecture we targeted in ASSERT was the priorityband architecture [19], a lightweight approach to hierarchical scheduling built on novel features of Ada 2005 [11].

That architecture permits a comparatively cost-effective deployment of multiple subsystems on one and the same computational node with guaranteed temporal and spatial isolation (hence attractive for processors with scarce computational power in comparison to e.g., civil and/or military avionics and automotive). The priority-band architecture can thus be used to realize partitioned distributed highintegrity real-time systems fully compliant with the RP.

In the priority-band architecture, the range of priorities available per node is divided in a set of contiguous nonoverlapping intervals called priority bands. Each task resident on a node is assigned a base priority which makes it belong to a specific priority band. Each subsystem (partition) is deployed on a single priority band and thus every task in that partition is assigned a priority in the range of the corresponding priority band. The structure of this architecture requires that local ordering is imposed on the priority-ranking of subsystems. This requirement does not necessarily translate in assigning a higher band to a highercriticality partition; rather, it uses the priority mechanism to contribute to attaining temporal isolation across partitions. Other mechanisms that we use to warrant temporal isolation include the enforcement of the minimum inter-arrival time of sporadic tasks and the monitoring of overruns against the WCET budget stipulated in the model and in the analysis.

Every single priority band has its own local scheduling policy which can be chosen among those specified by the language standard (fixed-priority preemptive, fixed-priority non-preemptive, EDF, round-robin). The global scheduler is a fixed-priority preemptive scheduler which ensures that at any time the CPU is granted to the highest-priority band with ready tasks in it. The selected partition elects a ready task for execution in accord with its local scheduling policy.
Thanks to the stack-based policy both intra-and interpartition communications may be permitted and can be carried out via protected objects as the RP requires.

div.head: Supported forms of schedulability analysis
div.p: Consideration of the three goals below was instrumental in deciding which forms of schedulability analysis to use in our explorative development: (i) to ensure that the chosen analysis theory would fit, whether by adaptation or new development, our reference architecture and its associated computational model; (ii) to be able to gradually arrive at applying the most advanced form of state-of-the-art analysis theory without this requiring major modifications to our metamodel and transformation infrastructure; (iii) to preserve the high level of modeling abstraction sought by MDE against the low level of details required by sophisticated scheduling analysis theory.

We wanted to equip the RCM with support for both feasibility and sensitivity analysis. For the former, we devised a form of response time analysis suited for the priority-band architecture [17] by adapting the equations of the analysis theory for the server-based architecture. In that work we showed that we could accommodate distinct equations for fixed-priority preemptive local scheduling [5] and EDF local scheduling [12] and that we could extend them where necessary to account for the use of shared resources.

In [17] we also evaluated the pessimism of that variant of schedulability analysis against the classical form of (flattened) response time analysis under the simplifying assumption that all local scheduling policies were FPPS. We showed that significant pessimism was incurred on account of the fact that all partitions with a criticality higher than the partition of the task under analysis are examined as blackbox monoliths, since only coarse-grained partition parameters (priority band, replenishment period and time budget) are used to calculate the worst-case interference, independently of the local scheduling policies of the partition of interest as well as of the interfering partitions.

A further result of interest on hierarchical scheduling with the priority-band architecture has recently been provided by [18]. That work shows that the benefits of EDF as local policy are modest even under high utilization of the computational node of interest (≥ 90%), well above what safety-margin prescriptions allow for the application domain of our interest. In fact, the potential gains of EDF are defeated by the global FPPS policy that dominates in the contribution to the feasibility conditions. On this account, the value of supporting EDF as a local scheduling policy in the kernel of our priority-band architecture becomes very dubious since the development costs and the space and time overheads we would incur, largely outweigh the benefit to be expected. Consequently, since we have opted to solely support FPP local scheduling, the resulting architecture is logically equivalent to a system with flat (as opposed to hierarchical) FPPS, the analysis can be optimized collapsing the equations to the form suited for those systems, as we hinted in the example discussed in [17].

The form of feasibility analysis discussed in [25] is a response time analysis for single-node systems with deadline equal to or shorter than task period or minimum interarrival, which accounts for all the run-time mechanisms of an RCM kernel that contribute to the response time of the task under analysis. To apply that baseline fine-grained analysis to distributed systems, we first extended it to allow deadlines to be greater than periods, using the arbitrary deadline analysis [23] by Tindell et al. that can account for the late release of an activation of a task to be delayed by its previous activation. Subsequently, we embedded the resulting equations and definitions in the holistic analysis by Tindell and Clark [24]. While much superior theories in terms of accuracy and control of pessimism exist to date, notably offset-based analysis [15], our prime concern was to gage the practicality of embedding that form of analysis in our MDE process: should the model be ill-equipped or unable to feed the equations of interest with trustworthy values then force-fitting even more advanced schedulability analysis in the RCM infrastructure would be more deceiving than productive. The result has been positive, which now permits to move toward more sophisticated analysis theory.

Response time analysis simply answers the question: "Is the system feasible?". For systems of realistic size however it becomes increasingly difficult to infer the causes of infeasibility for individual tasks since the equations provide little or no clues to the user in that regard. Sensitivity analysis, which answers the question: "Why is the system infeasible?", can defeat this problem by providing information on the consequences to be expected from changes in specific task attributes.

The work of Bini et al. [2] is an interesting example of sensitivity analysis for single-node fixed-priority preemptive systems. It provides sensitivity margins for periods as well as for computation times. In good fit with our requirements, the authors seek fine-grained sensitivity information by using the Linear Compute Time Model by Vestal [26], which no longer views tasks as monoliths, but rather regards them as the composition of distinct modules.

We have not managed to incorporate sensitivity analysis in RCM as yet. To complete that work, the underlying theory and equations should be extended to account for: (i) distributed systems with asynchronous message passing; (ii) shared resources, including the provision of sensitivity results on protected modules, that is, methods equipped with synchronization protocols; (iii) partition-based time budgets, which limit the feasible changes on WCET of their tasks; (iv) heterogeneous local scheduling policies.

div.head: RCM implementation status
div.p: We developed a proof-of-concept demonstrator of the whole RCM toolset. We used GMF, ATL and MOFscript [6] to develop the engines behind the graphical interface, the model transformations and the code generation respectively. We extended the MAST analysis tool [13] to support model-based analysis and the timing analysis equations we used. The decision to adopt the heavy-weight metamodeling strategy enabled us to incur comparatively low cost (64 graduate-student/months, from inception to industrial evaluation) to produce: 90 metaclasses to implement the RCM metamodel; 12,800 lines of ATL for model transformation; 7,500 lines of MOFscript to implement code generation; 7,500 lines of Java to complete the graphical editor (in addition to 150,000 lines generated automatically by GMF); and 5,500 lines of Ada for the required extensions to MAST.
Our current target platform is GNATforLEON 4 , an Ada 2005 compilation system for the LEON2 processor [9].

div.head: Expected benefits of RCM
div.p: With the promotion of RCM, we expected to attain comparative improvements in four key dimensions: consistency; automation; accuracy; round-trip analysis. In the following we discuss each of them in isolation.

div.head: Consistency
div.p: We want the semantics of the system model to be preserved in every supported view and at every level of abstraction, including source and executable code. To this end, RCM limits the design freedom strictly and also defines precise rules to be checked on the switch across model views.

The RCM metamodel ensures that the entities and constructs defined by the Ravenscar Computational Model also appear in the SAM natively. Assuming that the code generation engine generates Ravenscar-compliant code and that the compiler and kernel work as expected (which must be proven only once for any given language and platform target) we can assert full semantic equivalence between the user model, the run-time system and the SAM: analyzing the system description fed to the SAM thus is totally equivalent to analyzing the model as specified by the user and the analysis results are fully applicable to the run-time execution of the system as generated from the model.

We paid much attention to specifying and policing the rules that must apply on transition between model views, particularly between the user model and the SAM. The rules we defined precisely specify how each semantic entity is to be represented in each supported view. By way of example, Figure 1 shows how the simple communication of two software components can generate three distinct and increasingly complex SAM depending on the concurrent semantics specified for the provided interface (PI) at the server side.

div.head: Automation
div.p: Figure 1 shows what level of complexity may arise in the development of semantics-preserving relations between a simple user model and the SAM. While, in the example, the former simply includes two communicating components, the SAM may arrive at including multiple tasks, shared resources and synchronization protocols. To produce a semantics-preserving SAM by hand may thus rapidly become infeasible and undesirable. Proven automation is arguably better: we "calculate" the SAM from the user model and the deployment view and then make the result read-only in the user space. Proving the model transformation rules correct is done once, after which we may be certain that the model specified by the user is semantically equivalent to the SAM by construction. The SAM is automatically generated from the declarative specification of the concurrent semantics that decorates the user model (cf. section 3.1.1). Code is also automatically generated: the input models in this case are the user model, where the sequential semantics resides, and the SAM, where the schedulable entities emerge. In this manner we ensure that the analyzed model and the generated run-time system stay in sync and that the analysis results are trustworthy and applicable to both. In our approach the generation of the SAM does thus become a mandatory step prior to automated code generation. Admittedly, this requirement increases the computational cost of the code generation engine.

div.head: Accuracy
div.p: The first issue we cared for to cater for accurate analysis was that all of the middleware entities that would result from model transformation should be captured in the SAM. The middleware includes numerous elements that may affect the run-time behavior of the system in time and size (e.g.: daemon tasks waiting for incoming network messages). Those elements do not appear in any user views of the model because the middleware is normally accessed as a black-box API by the application. The model transformation that produces the SAM must thus incorporate all the schedulable entities that belong in the chosen middleware infrastructure, along with their relation with the original model entities. For example, a user component that issues a remote invocation may possibly interact with a client-side sender task at middleware level and this interaction must be present in the SAM. Stubs and skeletons undergo a similar treatment and are thus automatically incorporated in the SAM. This approach of course requires that full knowledge about the internal architecture and operation of every supported middleware infrastructure is made available to the development of the model transformations.

In addition to modeling the middleware, the SAM also has full knowledge of the timing overhead of the kernel primitives and uses it in the computation of the WCET attributes of all tasks. The C i attribute of task τ i is the total time cost to execute the worst-case execution path of that task: it therefore includes all services that the run-time support executes on behalf of that task. Thanks to its built-in knowledge, the SAM can statically determine which kernel primitives and how many times they must be accounted for in the determination of C i : the which question is answered by the activation type of the task (periodic or sporadic); the number of times question by the applicable critical instant that determines the interference incurred by task τ i .

Since all of the kernel mechanisms occur as explicit terms in the analysis (instead of being crudely collated in term C i ) and we can statically account for them thanks to the determinism of the RCM, we may treat the WCET of a task as the timing cost of the sequential modules that it calls during execution, much like Vestal views it.

div.head: Model-based round-trip analysis
div.p: Real-time attributes such as periods, ceilings and so forth, should normally be used to decorate the entities that populate the SAM. In RCM however, we solely allow the user to manipulate the PIM and not the SAM itself, and the former strictly precedes the latter. The user must therefore set real-time attributes on the PIM, but they have to take effect on the SAM. There is tension between the higher level of abstraction striven for in the PIM and the level of detail sought by the attributes that are input to the SAM. We solve that dilemma by inferring and/or calculating as many real-time attributes as we can and let the user set as few of them as possible, especially those that can be directly and sensibly related to the decoration of the provided interfaces of PIM entities. For example, the minimum separation time that should occur between any two subsequent executions of a given interface invocation, which in RCM is set on the server side. Other attributes for the user to set include: the concurrent kind of each provided operation (from which we infer the threads of control that must exist in the system) and their release pattern; the need for some synchronization protocol on access to a provided operation (which we may use to calculate ceiling values and blocking time); the WCET of each provided operation (which can be calculated on the sequential part of the relevant method) and the relative deadline (which is only required in case the interface in question was marked as requiring a thread executor).

The first step of the model-based round-trip analysis in RCM therefore consists in the automated creation of the SAM and the calculation of the required attributes off those set in the PIM by the user. The information on the hardware, the network topology, the physical and logical distribution of subsystems, and the description of the run-time platform for each computing node (run-time kernel and middleware) are all specified by the user in the deployment view of the system: the transformation weaves that information with the user model to generate the SAM, which is the sole input required for schedulability analysis to be performed.

When the analysis is complete, the results are first parsed and attached to the relevant SAM entities, and then propagated back to the PIM entities that they proceeded. The results are placed in specific read-only attributes that decorate the entity of interest. The round trip does not modify any of the attributes set by the user, so the automatic manipulation of the PIM cannot in any way overwrite the user requirements that it contains. The user can iterate the process at will until the system exhibits the worst-case behavior s/he deems most appropriate. A more detailed description of the round-trip mechanism in RCM can be found in [16].

div.head: Comparison
div.p: To compare RCM with MARTE and AADL (discounting plain UML2 as an unfit alternative) we focus on their fitness for model-based schedulability analysis rather than on their general modeling capabilities. RCM is obviously less expressive than MARTE and AADL, because it solely targets Ravenscar-compliant systems. Yet arguably RCM is ahead of them on the preservation of semantic consistency of model views across transformation as well as the finegrained accuracy it allows in the characterization of the execution platform, which are crucial prerequisites to attaining a faithful SAM and an equally trustworthy analysis.

The semantics-preserving approach of RCM may be realized in MARTE using OCL constraints. Similarly, the MARTE RTE Model of Computation and Communication can be used to infer the required schedulable resources, their interactions and the allocation of functional behavior.

The UML2/MARTE arguably is the ideal framework to exploit our RCM approach for other computational models. Three steps would have to be taken: (i) the relaxing, or strengthening, of OCL constrains; (ii) the adaptation of the model transformations generating the SAM; (iii) the accurate modeling of the run-time platform(s) of interest.

We doubt instead that the RCM approach could be as easily ported to AADL. That effort would in fact need considerable extensions to the syntax, semantics and metamodel infrastructure of the language on account of its insufficient model-level specification of run-time semantics, its lack of a semantically-integrated SAM and of (an equivalent to) OCL for enforcing consistency constraints.

div.head: Summary.
div.p: In this section we have illustrated the main properties of an approach to model-based schedulability analysis aggressively based on model transformation. From the standpoint of the MDE process, the automated production of the SAM should be augmented with support for iterative refinement of the user model (the PIM), ideally from as early as possible, so long as the user has meaningful value to set in the SAM-related attributes under his/her control. To what extent that may possible and what value can be drawn from the return of early round-trip analysis remains to be seen in real industrial projects. The experience gained in the case studies we carried out in the ASSERT project suggests that some adaptations of the industrial development process and some changes of the user mind-set may be needed to ripe the full potential of the RCM approach.

div.head: Evaluation
div.p: As stipulated earlier in this paper, we want to evaluate the fitness of our approach by examining: the amount of information required of the user at PIM level to enable RCM to automatically generate the SAM and whether that request may break or pollute the abstraction level of the PIM; the amount of pessimism (coarseness) introduced by the PIMonly visible modeling space of RCM, in comparison with AADL and MARTE which give direct access to the SAM.
Let us start from considering the semantics necessary for the SAM and its representation in an RCM user model.

Partial ordering of subsystems. On account of the priority-band architecture that we experimentally assumed as the default choice, when subsystems are first designed in the RCM development process, the user must specify a relative order among those deployed on one and the same computational node. We assign subsystems to priority bands and stack them in the priority range according to that order. We believe that this ordering may be established early in the process without extolling too much from the user.

Setting period, deadline, priority. Period, deadline, and priority are the attributes to be set on tasks. Since tasks only populate the SAM, those attributes are set by the user but only on the provided interfaces of the PIM components that, by RCM transformations, will produce tasks in the SAM. In other words, the relevant slots in the component attribute box become writable to the user only when the RCM rules require. Incidentally, the user is not requested to specify priority values but a relative order of urgency between those specific provided services of any given component. On creation of the SAM the PIM attributes are propagated downward as applicable. In particular: a deadline is attributed to the completion of any chain of PIM-level operations that have deferred interface attributes set at both ends; the relative order between subsystems and between tasks is woven with the description of the priority range available on the execution platform to produce the priority assignment to all tasks in the SAM. At that point, also the ceiling of protected objects may be automatically calculated.

Let us now look at when those attributes can be set. The period of operations typically depends on the frequency of the control laws that they compute. Occasionally they may also be dictated by the frequency of acquisitions from cycled buses and/or polled devices. A similar line of reasoning holds for end-to-end deadlines, which follow from end-to-end execution constraints. All of those elements of information are pertinent to the PIM as they concern individual (provided and required) services and concatenations thereof. We therefore contend that the user can determine initial estimates of those attributes early in the process and without reasoning much beyond the precincts of the PIM.

Calculating end-to-end execution flows and WCET. In RCM, tasks and shared resources are automatically generated in the SAM by model transformation. Each endto-end execution flow is completely inferred from intracomponents execution flows and component wirings: the former tell which required operations are invoked during the execution of a provided service; the latter specify which provided interface fulfills a required one. We expect the user to provide the specification of intra-component execution flows by partially modeling the action semantics at functional level, for example by sequence diagrams: such specification is usually part of the description/documentation of the functional dependencies of each operation. Component wiring instead is simply inferred by tracing a link between required and provided interfaces of components. In this manner, end-to-end execution flows are calculated following intra-component flows through the required interfaces to the wired components. The stereotypes attached to provided services tell whether the service is a task entry point, where model transformation maps the end for the incoming flows and the beginning for a new one. An alternative stereotype may specify whether a provided service should provide synchronized access: in that case, model transformation maps that service to an access to a protected object previously generated for the purpose. Model transformation does not cause any coarseness to the SAM, which is a blueprint representation of the PIM, just with tasks and shared resources in the place of software components.

WCET values are attached as descriptors to functional operations. To permit the reuse of functional specifications across different execution platforms, multiple WCET values may be attached to a single operation, each one applicable to a given target execution platform. We consequently do not pollute the PIM with platform-specific quantitative information, but rather allow its reuse across targets. The computational cost of end-to-end flows is determined by summing up the WCET of the functional operations that they traverse from their entry point to the point where they meet another entry point; model transformation selects perplatform WCET values following the deployment specification. Invocations to middleware/kernel primitives are automatically added to the flow cost (cf. section 3.2.3).

This approach is appropriate when the design of the system nears completion and the model inherently provides all of the information needed for timing analysis. When the model is early and partial, instead, very little information can be extracted automatically: for instance, incomplete functional specifications can hardly be used to automatically produce meaningful WCET estimates. In those circumstances it is advisable to allow the user to manually override WCET values in the PIM. The resulting coarseness of the SAM would then have to be mitigated by the intrinsically iterative nature of RCM development process. We may therefore contend that the approach we promote, based on the automated generation of the SAM to feed up complex and fine-grained analysis equations does not introduce intrinsic coarseness. Our model transformation introduces no semantic distortion in the generation of the SAM: tasks and shared resources are modeled by user stereotypes attached to component provided services; the end-to-end execution flows of tasks may be determined from usermodeled intra-component flows and component wirings; their computational cost accounts for both the WCET of operations included in the invocation chain and the interactions with middleware and kernel primitives.

div.head: Attribute
div.p: Our need for SAM-related information does not risk to pollute the PIM: platform-specific quantitative data that may be influenced by the user's choices (WCET, priority, period, deadline) are specified in the PIM using platformindependent semantics (e.g.: priorities are inferred from qualitative task ordering and multiple WCET values may be attached to individual operations) and translated down to the SAM. Conversely, platform-specific information that are not under user control (middleware modeling, kernel primitives) are automatically captured by the model transformation that generates the SAM.

The specific MDE process that we promote earns its advantages mostly from the guarantee of semantics preservation between PIM, SAM and run-time implementation, as well as from very accurate and fine-grained accounting of infrastructural overheads: all those features are crucial assets for raising the user confidence in sophisticated analysis results and they facilitate the quest for higher utilization of target processors above the current limit of 50%-60%. The focus on automation typical of MDE renders state-of-the-art equations for timing analysis usable and even attractive to the industrial community, even from the early phases of the development process. In those phases the use of sensitivity analysis coupled with model-based round-trip process may be especially useful to the user. By its very nature, sensitivity analysis marries well with the iterative process promoted by MDE and model-based round-trip is the effective mechanism to capitalize on its benefits and better exploit the potential of this theory across multiple iterations.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this paper we discussed the key elements that a modeldriven engineering process should exhibit to permit schedulability analysis in a completely automated fashion, without requiring the user to command the underlying analysis theory and its application: separation of concerns; semantics preservation across model views and transformations; automation, including the creation of the SAM; accuracy, which ensues from finely-specified computational model and middleware infrastructure of choice.

The proof-of-concept tools we developed were used in real-scale industrial case studies which showed that the iterative nature of the MDE development process facilitates the use of advanced analysis equations, especially if capable of sensitivity reasoning.

Our research in this field will progress in two distinct directions. Firstly, we want to apply more advanced schedulability theory that promises to incur less pessimism. Secondly, now that we have obtained very encouraging industrial returns on the vision and core concepts of RCM, we plan to migrate it to MARTE so as to attain wider applicability and larger opportunities of collaboration, owing to the OMG standard status of MARTE.
